title: Edge-case Sales Heatmap — LLM API competitors
content:
Purpose:
Quick-reference heatmap and tactical plays for customer conversations where competitors pitch "best-in-class" LLM APIs. Target audience: AE/SE pre-sales and SDRs prepping discovery calls and PO approvals.

Topline thesis (1-liner):
Customers choose inference partners on predictable economics + operational guarantees, not just raw model claims. Show them how Redwood maps to their risk/cost/latency constraints in edge cases.

How to use this doc:
- Skim the heatmap if you have <5 minutes.
- Use the ‘Edge objections’ table in live calls.
- Copy the demo checklist into your sandbox runbook.

Competitor heatmap (at-a-glance strengths/weaknesses):
Axes: Performance (latency throughput), Cost predictability, Enterprise controls (VPC/KMS/SLA), Feature parity (streaming, function-calls), Degradation resilience (fallbacks, regional capacity)
Legend: Strong / Moderate / Weak / Risk

1) Competitor A: large public model-first API- Performance: Strong at bursty single requests (low p50), Weak at consistent sustained throughput (cost spikes)- Cost predictability: Weak — opaque tiering, egress-style add-ons- Enterprise controls: Moderate — SSO and basic VPC, limited KMS options- Feature parity: Strong (lots of newer model features)- Degradation resilience: Risk — single-region dependency, limited fallback policies
Sales play: Call out cost variability for sustained workloads. Ask for 30-day token usage pattern and show Redwood’s Dedicated pricing vs expected spike cost.

2) Competitor B: infra-first vendor (self-host/managed hybrid)- Performance: Moderate (good on well-tuned infra, but ops risk)- Cost predictability: Moderate — you may be responsible for underutilized reserved instances- Enterprise controls: Strong (on-prem options)- Feature parity: Moderate — slower to adopt new model features- Degradation resilience: Moderate — depends on customer ops maturity
Sales play: Offer Redwood Private as lower-risk alternative with our ops/SLAs and a migration path (pilot then on-prem). Emphasize telemetry/rollouts for safe upgrades.

3) Competitor C: low-cost commodity API- Performance: Weak at scale; high variance latency- Cost predictability: Strong on small volume; weak for scale due to hidden limits- Enterprise controls: Weak — poor logs and audit- Feature parity: Weak — limited streaming, function calling- Degradation resilience: Weak
Sales play: Push reliability and observability. Small-dollar wins are fine, but for product features put Redwood’s SLAs and tracing on the table.

Edge objections (table) — use on calls as a checklist:
Objection: "Your pricing is higher than X"
- Root cause: customer comparing list price vs hidden fees elsewhere
- Quick rebuttal (30s): "We make unit economics predictable — our billing + batching + KV caching reduces per-token cost on sustained workloads; we can run a modeled estimate from your sample traces in 48h."
- Follow-up ask: "Can you share 7–14 day traffic traces or representative prompt set? We'll return a modeled cost delta."

Objection: "We already have a cloud provider offering model endpoints."
- Root cause: inertia + perceived integration cost
- Rebuttal: "Most cloud endpoints optimize for model access not inference economics. Redwood gives the same API across hosted/dedicated/private so you can standardize client-side without lock-in."
- Demo hook: Show identical SDK + route-level rollouts in Console (5 min demo).

Objection: "We need on-prem for compliance — your managed cloud won't work."
- Root cause: regulatory requirement or overcautious security team
- Rebuttal: "We support Private with customer-managed control plane and an air-gapped on-prem package. Customers typically start with a dedicated VPC pilot and then transition to full Private if needed."
- Follow-up: Offer an architecture sketch and SOW template.

Objection: "Your latency isn't as good as competitor X in their demo."
- Root cause: cherry-picked demo metrics / short p50 focus
- Rebuttal: "We optimize for p99 and throughput using continuous batching, KV cache, and sequence-aware kernel selection. Let's look at your latency SLA needs (p50 vs p95 vs p99) and run a 2-hour stability test."

Tactical rebuttal snippets (copy-paste friendly):
- Pricing: "Share a sample week of traffic and we'll model cost + performance delta; many customers see 20–40% unit-cost savings after batching and cache."
- Model features: "We maintain a curated model catalog and provide version pinning and automated fallback to compatible variants during capacity events."
- Security: "Full audit logs, KMS integration, and optional private control plane — we can include HSM options in enterprise SOW."

Demo checklist (30-minute sequence for AE/SE):
1) Quick setup (3m): show same SDK call against hosted and a pinned dedicated model.
2) Observability (5m): Console trace for a sample route; highlight token-level cost and latency waterfall.
3) Rollouts (5m): Create a canary route and show automatic fallback to backup variant.
4) Cost controls (5m): Demonstrate batching suggestions and a simulated workload showing unit-cost delta.
5) Private path (7m): Walk high-level architecture for VPC/private deployment + typical timeframes and SOW.
Notes: always capture customer SLA requirements (p50/p95/p99, throughput qps) before demo.

Technical callouts for SEs (short):
- Serving: continuous batching + KV cache reduces hot-starts for chat workloads
- Kernels: dynamic kernel selection for mixed sequence lengths improves throughput up to 2–3x on some models
- Quantization: we recommend selective quantization for embedding-heavy flows; we can pre-validate on 500k tokens
- Routing: policy-based routing (latency vs cost vs region) + automatic fallback to compatible variants during regional saturation

Traps to avoid (internal notes):
- Don’t promise exact cost savings without sample data — customers will hold us to numbers.
- Avoid deep model-quality debates vs proprietary providers; instead, point to evals and historical regressions monitoring.
- Don’t position Redwood as just "cheaper" — emphasize predictability, observability, and deployment flexibility.

Sales plays by buyer persona (brief):
- Platform/Infra buyer: lead with Dedicated capacity + SLAs + autoscaling policies. Show capacity planning table.
- Product/ML buyer: lead with runtime features (KV cache, rollouts, evals) and model catalog. Offer a quality-regression alert trial.
- Security/Compliance: lead with Private/VPC + KMS/HSM options and audit logs. Offer architecture review.
